This is the duck breast you make when you want the night to feel intentional. Not fussy. Not chaotic. Just a slow-build kind of impressive that makes the whole apartment feel like a plan.

Because the secret here is patience: a **3-day miso cure** that quietly seasons the meat, dries the surface, and sets you up for the kind of **shatter-crisp skin** people assume you only get at restaurants.
You’ll rinse the cure off, render the fat, sous vide for perfect doneness, then hit it with a high-heat sear and a torch (or grill) for blistery edges. It’s bold, clean, and *deeply* savory.

items: **Prep time:** 20 minutes active (plus 72 hours curing)
**Cook time:** 20–30 minutes active
**Total time:** About 3 days + 45 minutes
**Servings:** 3 (or 2 very generously)
**Difficulty:** Medium (high reward, very doable)

blocks.text: Why You’ll Love This 3-Day Miso Duck

items: **Skin that actually crackles.** The cure + drying + render + blast of heat is the full crisp pipeline.
**Juicy, perfectly rosy meat.** Sous vide takes the stress out.
**Big umami without heavy sauce.** Shiro miso keeps it nutty and clean.
**Date-night friendly timing.** The longest part happens while you’re doing literally anything else.
3 duck breasts, skin-on (about 250–350g each)
3⅜ tbsp (about 52–53g) **white (shiro) miso paste**
1½ tsp + a heavy pinch **kosher salt** (about 9g)
1 tbsp + ⅛ tbsp **mirin**
1⅛ tsp **honey or sugar** (optional, but helps browning)
**Julienned green onions**
**Maldon salt** (or any flaky salt)

blocks.text: Shopping Notes (So You Don’t Overthink It)

items: **Duck breasts:** Look for plump breasts with an even fat cap. Smaller breasts cook faster, but the method is the same.
**Shiro miso:** White miso is sweet-ish and gentle. Red miso can work, but it’s louder and saltier. If you swap, use a touch less salt.
**Mirin:** Adds sweetness and gloss. If you don’t have it, use a tiny splash of sake or rice vinegar plus a pinch more sugar.
**Flaky salt:** This is your last-second “chef move.” A few flakes right at the end changes everything.

blocks.text: Mix miso, salt, mirin, and honey into a **thick, spreadable paste**.

items: Pat duck breasts very dry.
Score the skin in a crosshatch pattern **without cutting into the meat**.
Coat each breast evenly in a **1–2 mm** layer of the miso paste.
Place on a wire rack over a tray.
Refrigerate **uncovered for 72 hours** in the coldest/back spot of your fridge.
Rinse/scrape off the miso under cold water.
Pat **extremely** dry.
Place duck **skin-side down in a cold cast iron**.
Turn heat to **medium**.
Render **6–8 minutes**, until the skin is golden and a good amount of fat has pooled.
Transfer to a rack. Pour off and save the rendered duck fat.
Vacuum bag duck **skin-up** (no added fat needed).
Cook at **58°C / 136°F for 2 hours**.
Ice bath **15 minutes**.
Pat bone-dry.
Optional (but great): fridge uncovered **30 minutes** to dry the surface.
Heat cast iron until **smoking hot**.
Add a small spoon of rendered duck fat.
Sear:
**Skin-side down:** 90 seconds to 2 minutes (press flat)
**Flesh side:** 30–45 seconds
**Edges/ends:** 20–30 seconds each
Transfer to a rack to drain.
**Torch:** 60–90 seconds, sweeping all surfaces until blistered.
**Grill:** hot grate, mostly indirect, 2–3 minutes for char/smoke.
Rest **5 minutes**, lightly tented.
Slice thin on a bias and fan out.
Top with **julienned green onions** and a few flakes of **Maldon salt**.

blocks.text: Expert Tips (So It Comes Out Perfect)

items: **Dryness is the whole game.** After rinsing, after sous vide, and before the final sear: keep patting until the surface is truly dry.
**Don’t rush the render.** Medium heat first so the fat melts out without scorching.
**Sear fast.** Sous vide already nailed doneness. The last sear is for texture and color.
**Use a rack, not a plate.** A plate traps steam and softens the skin.

blocks.text: It’s the point. You *can* do 24–48 hours, but 72 gives better seasoning and a drier surface for crisping.
No, but it’s the easiest way to guarantee juicy duck with a short, aggressive final sear. If you skip it, use a thermometer and finish in a low oven after rendering, then sear quickly.
**Can I cure more than 3 breasts at once?**
Yes. Just keep them on a rack with space between so air can circulate.
Any leftover miso will scorch during the final high-heat sear and taste bitter.
Usually one of two things: the surface wasn’t dry enough, or the pan wasn’t hot enough for the final sear.
**Cure (72 hours):** Mix miso, salt, mirin, honey. Dry duck, score skin, coat 1–2 mm thick. Fridge uncovered on rack 72 hours. Rinse off, pat extremely dry.

**Cook:** Render skin in cold pan → medium heat 6–8 min. Sous vide 58°C/136°F 2 hours. Ice bath 15 min, dry, optional fridge 30 min. Re-sear in ripping-hot pan: skin 90 sec–2 min, flesh 30–45 sec, edges 20–30 sec. Torch 60–90 sec or grill 2–3 min.
**Finish:** Rest 5 min. Slice. Top with julienned green onions + Maldon salt.
